utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If there are no preliminaries, then could temporarily could the curtains be down so that the witness can enter the courtroom, and could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness RM081. I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have -- is there any problem with the sounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear this noise, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the curtains that are pulled up. We'll wait for a second until its over. Witness RM081, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. RM081.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we'd ended off in private session last week and I'd like to go back to private session to finish off the questions that might reveal the personal nature of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Because it's important, Mr. Stojanovic, could you please again -- perhaps I summarise. You said when Mr. Mladic left the courtroom, he insisted that time would be given to briefly consult with you and also instructed you -- he insisted that you should not be in the courtroom if he is not in the courtroom, and that you tried to explain to him your duties and obligations, and that you had no further chance to talk to him during the short break, and that is why you're asking to enable you to have a very brief contact with Mr. Mladic. Is there anything you'd like to add? I summarised and to some extent repeated what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. According to the rules, the security did not allow us to have any further contact with Mr. Mladic, and we are now in a vice between the obligations that we have and the demands of our client. That's why we're asking you to give us a little time to clarify the situation we're in with Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. I'll consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the fact that you could not consult with Mr. Mladic is entirely due to his behaviour. That is what caused the problem. We will take the usual break in ten minutes from now, which is -- meanwhile, consider what your duties are. If you would decide at this moment to leave the courtroom, then we would continue, because we consider it a waiver of Mr. Mladic. Now, of course you have a few possibilities. One of them is that one of you consult with Mr. Mladic and that meanwhile we'll continue in court. I'm not suggesting what you're supposed to do. You know entirely -- you can decide for yourself, but that is how we look at it. Apart from that, you know that Mr. Mladic has an opportunity to follow the proceedings on a screen at this very moment. Of course, whether he uses that opportunity is a different matter, but he has an opportunity to do that. So therefore, we'll continue until 10.30 and then you'll have an opportunity to consult with him, or one of your colleagues, of course, at this moment could already -- or I think ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you know that for members of the team to cross-examine witnesses, the presence of counsel is required, but you are the three of you. So even if counsel is here and if Mr. Ivetic further cross-examines the witness, then still Mr. Petrusic could consult with Mr. Mladic if he wishes. That's the situation. That's how we'll proceed. Then, Mr. Ivetic, you may continue your cross-examination and we'll take a break in eight minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more thing, with your leave, Your Honour. Could you allow Mr. Petrusic to leave and get into contact with Mr. Mladic and the rest of us will be in the same position in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrusic can take any instructions as he wishes and consult with Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could return to private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We return into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Defence is hereby informed that the removal of Mr. Mladic from the courtroom lasts until the conclusion of the examination of the present witness. Mr. Mladic is allowed to re-enter the courtroom for the next witness. We also understood that Mr. Mladic would prefer to return to the -- to the UNDU. The Chamber would seek, if Mr. Mladic wants to return, a clear expression of a waiver to attend the proceedings for the beginning of the testimony of the next witness if Mr. Mladic would wish to return. Now, whether or not he could return at this moment and what it takes to bring him back earlier than scheduled is something the Chamber is not competent. The only thing we could say is that if under those circumstances and with a clear waiver that if he would be returned to the UNDU earlier than scheduled, that the Chamber would not oppose that, but whatever extra efforts it takes, the Chamber is not aware of it, and the Chamber certainly not does -- does certainly not instruct anyone to bring him any earlier to the UNDU. Is that clear, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is completely clear, Your Honour. And if you'll allow me to, I would like to present the view and position of the Defence following our conversation with Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would briefly explain. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's relevant to this matter. Based upon my discussions with the Defence earlier today, it seems that they will be concluding their cross-examination mid-session of this session. At present we only have two questions. The next witness is somewhat pressed for time and is available to begin immediately, so I would ask that there be no delay occasioned by this going back and forth to the prison if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. No. Again, if Mr. Mladic would be returned to the UNDU, then it would be on the basis of a clear waiver to not attend the beginning of the testimony of the next witness. That should be clear. Mr. Stojanovic, very briefly, because we have spent already quite some time on the matter. So if you could inform us in one or -- one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, over the break we analysed the rules governing situations such as this one. We conveyed the contents of these rules to our client, Mr. Mladic, who asked that we represent his interests in the courtroom. He stood by his position and insisted that we convey his sentiments to you that he was no longer capable of restraining his emotions, be they tears or laughter, given the condition he is in, and he made it clear to us that he did not wish us to proceed with the examination of the witness outside of his presence. He asked that should this be the course of action chosen, that we should withdraw from the courtroom as well. We presented to him the views of the Chamber on this, and he said that we should let it be known that if this sort of situation will continue, he will refrain from taking his medication and go on a hunger strike, and he insisted that we should convey this to you. Now, as for your order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, sending this kind of message is -- is not, I think, something that is the appropriate time and the appropriate moment to do, but we've heard it. It's there. Our order, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me conclude by saying this, Your Honours: In view of your decision whereby Mr. Mladic should be absent from the rest of the examination of this witness, I can inform you that we will conclude our examination at this moment. We have no further questions for him. Now, if the Prosecution have any additional questions, we could conclude this witness and allow Mr. Mladic to return to the courtroom again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if Mr. Mladic is unable to control his emotions that amounts to interference with witnesses, because a clear laughter in the presence of the witness is interference, and the Chamber will take the same position for the future. So therefore, Mr. Mladic is urged to control his emotions to avoid consequences as we have seen today. I do understand that you conclude your -- hereby conclude your cross-examination. Then we'll have the witness escorted into the courtroom. Ms. D'Ascoli, would you have questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the curtains be put down and could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness RM081, we'll wait for a second for the curtains to be pulled up again. Meanwhile, Ms. D'Ascoli, could we remain in open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I would need us to go in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. D'Ascoli, I think that part of what we dealt with in private session perhaps would have been better dealt with in open session, especially your questions about the questions that were put to the witness in preparing for statements or earlier testimony, and whether that was specific about Mr. Mladic. That's hereby put on the record in a summarius format. Then I gave an opportunity to the Defence to put further questions to the witness triggered by the re-examination. The Defence had no further questions. Witness RM081, this ends your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once the curtains are down, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may take a couple of minutes to remove the screens and to prepare for the return of Mr. Mladic into the courtroom. We take a break of two minutes, and the Chamber expects then Mr. Mladic to be escorted back into the courtroom. --- Break taken at 11.32 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I established that Mr. Mladic has not returned to the courtroom, although he will be given an opportunity to do so. The Chamber interprets this as an explicit waiver to attend the proceedings. If, Mr. Stojanovic, there is anything wrong in the interpretation of the behaviour of Mr. Mladic, then you have half a second -- well, not half a second, of course, but you have a brief opportunity to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have just returned from the room where Mr. Mladic is. He is lying down. He feels very unwell. He would like his pressure to be checked before his return to the courtroom. He is lying down, and I'm conveying his wish to you now that he have his blood pressure measured, and he certainly does not look at all well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we did not hear from you whether Mr. Mladic, apart from his condition at this moment, is willing to return to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I believe I said so. He would like to come back, but I conveyed every word of his to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber rules as follows: We'll continue with the proceedings. If it would turn out after the measurement of the blood pressure of Mr. Mladic that there would be a sound medical reason not to attend, the Chamber will consider whether or not to restart the testimony of the witness who is next to be called by the Prosecution. If there are no sound medical reasons, the Chamber even exceptionally will allow Mr. Mladic to return to the courtroom during the testimony. The Chamber takes as a rule that if Mr. Mladic for any specific reason is absent from the courtroom due to his own will, that we would allow him to return to the courtroom after a break and not to interrupt the proceedings. As matters stand now and also in view of a long history of Mr. Mladic not feeling well where no sound medical reasons were found for him not to be able to attend, we'll proceed at this moment, and if matters are different today, we'll certainly -- upon an application, we will consider whether or not to restart or to take appropriate remedy for Mr. Mladic having missed part of the proceedings. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I understand that he is -- he's prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Vanderpuye, I -- the Chamber noted that the number of associated exhibits is far beyond the guidance of the Chamber. I see that the grey ones, which you usually would not use, the shaded items, are in the minority and there is still a huge number of associated exhibits, which certainly does not fit in the guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Would you like me to respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at this moment. The only thing is that you are aware that the Chamber considers this not to be in accordance with the guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that you should take appropriate action to be within the limits again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tucker, I take it. I apologise for not paying proper attention to your entry into the courtroom. Mr. Tucker, before you give evidence the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Tucker. Mr. Tucker, you'll first be examined by Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Vanderpuye is counsel for the Prosecution. You'll find him to your right. You may proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning to you, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good morning to you, Mr. Tucker. Mr. Tucker, first would you prefer to be addressed as Mr. Tucker or Colonel Tucker?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker will be fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well. As you know my name is Kweku Vanderpuye, and before we get started I just wanted to remind to try to keep your voice up, speak a little bit more slowly than you would otherwise so that it'll give the interpreters a chance to keep up with us as we speak the same language. For the sake of the record, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: My name is Pyers William Tucker.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter 28446, and while that's coming up let me ask you: Do you recall having provided the Office of the Prosecutor a witness statement on 10 May 2010 -- or, rather, dated 10 May, 2010?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document that's in -- on the screen in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It's the statement of which I compiled and then eventually signed on the 10th of May, 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page of this document, page 75. Do you recognise the signature there? Is it yours?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you undertook the acknowledgement that is indicated on this page as to the truth of the statement in question; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall providing certain corrections to that statement during the course of your testimony in the trial of Radovan Karadzic on 17 January 2012?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, that is at transcript pages 23192 through 23194. I have a summary of those corrections which we have marked as 65 ter 28452, which I would like to tender in addition to the statement, but first let me finish the qualifications for 92 ter purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, have you had an opportunity to review your testimony in the Karadzic case and in particular the corrections of which I'm discussing just now?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you confirm that your statement, subject to the corrections to which you testified in the Karadzic case, is accurate and truthful to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And let me just ask, does your statement as corrected therefore fairly and accurately reflect what you would say if you were to be examined today on the same issues?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would tender both the statement as well as the corrections, and in view of the Court's position concerning the associated exhibits, I expect we can deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to the statement and the corrections that have been marked a separate 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement document 28446 becomes Exhibit P317, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P317 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And correction [indiscernible] 28452 becomes Exhibit P318, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P318 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Vanderpuye, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a brief summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: From October 1992 until March 1993, Colonel Pyers Tucker, a British Army officer, served with UNPROFOR as military assistant to General Philippe Morillon, the commander of UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Colonel Tucker's evidence concerns the siege of Sarajevo and the ethnic cleansing of Eastern Bosnia by the Bosnian Serb Army during his tour. He witnessed shelling and sniping in Sarajevo, which he describes as terroristic and intimidatory and requiring co-ordinated military operations achievable only with the approval of the VRS chain of command. His evidence also discusses the extreme humanitarian toll borne by Sarajevo's civilian population. In March 1993, Colonel Tucker travelled with General Morillon to Eastern Bosnia, including Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica. VRS operations against these Muslim-held areas were underway and forcing civilians from their homes. Colonel Tucker witnessed the desperate humanitarian situation of thousands of refugees as they fled their villages and streamed into Srebrenica. He describes the VRS' shelling of columns of Muslim refugees making their way to safety, their shelling of UN forces as they distributed aid in Konjevic Polje, and their shelling of a humanitarian air-lift during an evacuation of the wounded. Colonel Tucker accompanied General Morillon to Srebrenica where Muslim refugees blocked them from leaving, fearing that upon their departure the VRS would shell them as they had recently done in Konjevic Polje. Colonel Tucker personally accompanied General Morillon to meetings with General Mladic, President Karadzic, and other senior political and military leaders of the warring factions in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He kept notes of these meetings and drafted reports for General Morillon, for UNPROFOR headquarters, and others. His evidence describes these meetings and the issues consistently raised by General Morillon with Bosnian Serb leaders in relation to the siege of Sarajevo, freedom of movement of UN forces, and the delivery of humanitarian aid convoys and resources, which were repeatedly and deliberately obstructed by Bosnian Serb forces. That concludes my summary, Mr. President, and I do have a number of questions for Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, in your statement you noted that the repair of utilities in and around Sarajevo featured prominently on General Morillon's agenda. You mentioned that in a number of different areas in your statement, in particular paragraphs 26, 116, and 286. What I'd like to know is how often were these issues raised with the Bosnian Serb leadership to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: They were raised in virtually every meeting that will the Mixed Military Working Group had with the Bosnian Serbs, and they were raised in most meetings that General Morillon had with members of the Bosnian Serb leadership. If you look at my testimony in this case and others, you will see multiple references to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What was your perception of the attitude shown by the Bosnian Serb leadership with respect to the repair of utilities affecting Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The attitude was one of controlling a tap and drip feeding repairs so that they could not accused of blocking them completely, but equally never fully addressing the situation of very limited utilities being available to the population of the Sarajevo; that is, gas for heating, electricity for heating and lighting and cooking, and water.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were these matters raised separately with the political and military leadership, or were they raised simultaneously with both, and did you observe any difference in the results on the ground as a result of either?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: These matters were raised with both political leadership in order to get agreement in principle and with military leadership in order to execute specific repairs at a time, place, location, and to arrange a necessary cease-fire for the engineers to get access to whatever it was that needed repair.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when it was raised as between one or the other, that is the military leadership or the political leadership, did you observe any difference in the results that were realised on the ground?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No. Very limited progress was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned at paragraph 116 in your statement that the Bosnian Serbs, that is the participants of the Mixed Military Working Group, in meetings with Mladic, Gvero, and sometimes Tolimir, invariably wanted a quid pro quo before allowing any repairs to utilities. I just wanted to clarify what do you mean in the context of a quid pro quo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: What I meant was that in these negotiations, the Bosnian Serb side would want agreement or acceptance of some other issue before they were willing to approve or agree to a particular repair being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you believe that in your dealings or General Morillon's dealings with the Serb leadership that they undertook a genuine interest in working to resolve the problems surrounding the repair or maintenance of utility services to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We believed that they, when it suited them, would address the issues, but most of the time that despite saying that they were trying their best, that they were firmly keeping the tap closed, to use my previous analogy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter 2353. And what we should see are the minutes from the 16th National Assembly session, dated 12 May 1992. And what I'd like to do is to go first to page 31 in the English. And I think it should also be 31 in the B/C/S. And just for the record, before we move on to the substance of what I'm getting at, we can see here at the top of the page that General Mladic is present and is recorded speaking. Do you see that, Mr. Tucker?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do now is to go to page 38 in the English and 36 in the B/C/S. It is rather small, but if we go to the bottom quarter of the page in the English, we can see General Mladic saying the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could it be, please, enlarged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should seek confirmation with the witness whether he's able to read it or not or whether it would be more comfortable for him to have it enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, I'm going to refer you to about ten lines up from the bottom of the page where it says, "We should not say," and there's a semicolon, and it says, "We should not say we will destroy Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. It reads that: "We should not say we will destroy Sarajevo. We need Sarajevo. We're not going to say that we're going to destroy the power supply pylons or turn off the water supply. No, because that would get America out of its seat. But, gentlemen, please find, well, one day there is no water at all in Sarajevo. What is it? We do not know. Damage? We should fix it. No, we will fix it slowly. And the same with the electrical power, Zadar, Sibenik, and Split. They disconnected the army's power supply. The army had none for six months, but I told them while I am here you will not get it and they didn't, apart from when I felt like letting them have some or when that president, the one for political affairs, that Viktor Andreev. Therefore, we have to wisely tell the world it was they who were shooting, hit the transmission line, and the power went off. They were shooting at the water supply facilities. There was a power cut" -- if we can go to the next page. In both. In both languages, please. "There was a power cut at such and such a place. We're doing our best --"

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I'm no longer looking at the text that you're reading out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we should be on the next page at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It takes a second to move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have to go to the top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that we are on -- we should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Page 39 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 39 e-court page in English, starting with "... cut at such and such a place." There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It reads: "There was a power cut at such and such a place. We're doing our best repairing this. That is what diplomacy is. And not like yesterday when this smart man in Nevesinje, I do not want to offend him, when he said, when I have exposed their goals, what's the point in exposing their goals when it is the Vatican setting their goals for them." In terms of what General Mladic says at this Assembly session concerning the utilities, in particular asserting that the other side was shooting at them, severed the transmission line and so on and so forth, does that -- is that consistent with your experience in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is exactly what was happening in Sarajevo and is exactly what I meant when I described controlling the tap and letting a little bit out every now and then but never opening the tap.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you believe at the time that you were in Sarajevo with General Morillon -- or, rather, in Bosnia-Herzegovina with General Morillon, that you were dealing fairly and honestly with the Serb -- Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We believed we were dealing with them in a very difficult situation. What exactly their motives and how truthful they were being to us was always something we were never entirely sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What do you make of that now that you see what General Mladic said on the 12th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It confirms the most negative assumptions that we considered at the time in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 90 through 91, you refer to a few different concepts with respect to the use of artillery in Sarajevo, in particular, terrorism, random shelling, punitive shelling. And what I'd like for you to do if you could is just explain what you mean by those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, is counsel going to be tendering the exhibit that we just discussed? Because I have a submission that I have just been confirmed to make on that document on the evidence that was led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was looking at the document, and I wondered, but perhaps I've missed it, where exactly it says that Mr. Mladic is speaking, because I see on other pages clearly indicated who is the speaker, whereas here I'm trying to find on page 38 or the previous pages where it is Mr. Mladic that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the -- it begins at page 31 in English, 31 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have a look. Thirty-one, you are referring to -- let me see. We have -- I have on page 30, that's the previous page, Mr. Krajisnik speaking, then Mr. Mijatovic, then again Mr. Krajisnik at the end of page 30. Now -- yes. I see it's slightly different indicated compared to the others. Yes, it's clear to me. Mr. Ivetic, do I understand you well that you wanted to object, perhaps, to this document being tendered, but it has not been tendered yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know, Your Honours, but it has not been identified as a document for this document until -- well, yesterday, at 5.00, and the e-mail that we sent -- received this morning at 8.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Van --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I've raised this before with Your Honours. Seven days is what your guidance is. I don't know what that guidance means since it is not being followed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The guidance means guidance. Mr. Vanderpuye --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- do you want to tender this document and to tender the document in its entirety, and when was that you indicated to the Defence that you would use it, this document, which is far prior to the arrival of the witness in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I told the Defence about the use of the document yesterday as Mr. Ivetic has indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- following my proofing of the witness which occurred yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's number one. Number two is I don't need to tender it through the witness. I notified the Defence that I intended to use it with the witness. It is referred to in an expert report and then there is other evidence that will come in with respect to it, so I don't need to tender it through the witness although it is my intention to use it with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, there is no intention to tender this document only apparently to read small portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed, Your Honour. And I thought the guidance was with documents that were going to be used with the witness. That was my understanding of it. That's what we've been doing with all of our lists. Any document that we want to use with the witness is on our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber wants to consider this objection against the use of the document because that's, Mr. Ivetic, I understand what is your objection, but to first take a break, and then we have 20 minutes to discuss it, and you have 20 minutes to prepare for what -- for the remainder of the morning. We take a break, and we resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I -- if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do see that General Mladic is now in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to establish that. Mr. Mladic returned to the courtroom. The Chamber was informed that Mr. Mladic's blood pressure was measured by security and by the ICTY medical unit nurse and that it was found to be acceptable according to the ICTY nurse to follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. President, whether or not the Defence has an application or whether the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vanderpuye --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if the Defence has an application we'll hear from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we leave it at the time being as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: One last thing, Mr. President, I was wondering if the Chamber is prepared to dispose of the issue raised by Mr. Ivetic at this time or whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has considered it. The Chamber has established that the document is -- may be have been put to the witness during proofing, that's fine, but it's -- first of all, it's a document dealing with what happened in May when the witness has not -- had not yet arrived. Second, the only thing you asked him, whether it was consistent with what he experienced. Now, what we read from the statement and whether that is consistent what we find here, we don't even need the witness for that. It's not a novelty coming up in proofing, because I take it that the Prosecution has put this to the witness, and therefore the Prosecution now creates the novelties by putting documents to the witness apparently, and that is not how the guidance should be understood as any new thing coming up during proofing. Is that clear Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Not exactly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what we have -- we'll later explain it to you in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you're supposed not to use it any further. I don't know whether you had any further questions. And it is without prejudice as to the tendering of this document under different circumstances when using it under different circumstances, but you're supposed not to use this document any further with the witness and the ruling of the Chamber is also that you shouldn't have used it as a matter of fact. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With your permission, I would like to address this matter following my examination of the witness, because I think it goes to a very important point with respect to the use of exhibits and the proofing process that we follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber certainly will consider whether to hear any further submissions on the matter both from the Defence and the Prosecution and in which format to do that and whether it should be done orally or in writing is a matter we'll further consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, in your statement at paragraphs 90 through 91, you refer to a few different concepts with respect to the use of artillery. As concerns punitive shelling, can you tell the Chamber what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: By punitive shelling, what I mean is the shelling of a suburb of the town from which previously an attack had been made against Bosnian Serb lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would that shelling be considered defensive in the circumstances under which you observed it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That shelling would not be considered defensive as it was not necessary. It was shelling which was carried out after the attack and after the military operations in order to defend against that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also characterize some of the shelling that you observed as terrorism or terroristic. Could you describe what is meant by that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: What I mean by that is single shells being fired somewhere into the city of Sarajevo to no observable or obvious military intent. The only observable consequence of the shells are to make the civilian population very anxious and concerned about the possibility of high explosives raining out of the sky at complete random. And the Bosnian Serbs must have known that this was the case, and as I said, there was no observable military intent with these individual, single shells coming in, so therefore the inference was that it was done primarily to terrorise and cow the population, the civilians living in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I waited to see if this was going to be linked somehow to the witness's own personal observations of specific incidents. It has not. I submit that this is improper expert testimony that has not been qualified under Rule 94 bis nor tendered under Rule 94 bis and is now giving expert-type testimony of the type that we have objected to in our response to the Rule 92 ter motion for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Vanderpuye, with a 73-page statement, where is the terroristic? Could you guide me, because the punitive shelling you indicated was paragraph 91. By the way, the questions you have put to the witness in respect of the punitive shelling, nothing arose which was not already very clear from the statement itself, but where do we have the terrorist?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe we have it in paragraph 90 and 91.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ninety and 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you bear with me, I'll give you the reference for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's in 90. Yes. Then, Mr. Ivetic, in paragraph 90 it's directly linked to the use of artillery in the battles for Otes, which seems to be not just a general statement but -- but perhaps Mr. Vanderpuye could further explore with the witness to what extent there is a basis in his personal experience which led the witness and perhaps others to describe it in the way they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then this paragraph was objected to in our response in the Rule 92 ter as being expert type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not exactly how -- sure how to address Mr. Ivetic's objection. I don't see that it has any foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am prepared, however, to proceed on your guidance and to put it to the witness on what basis he drew the inference that is indicated in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least to link the description and the qualifications to his personal experience on specific incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you've described now what you meant by the terroristic use of artillery. First, can you tell us how it is that you arrived at that specific conclusion with respect to what you observed on the ground?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: During my time in Sarajevo, there was continual shell-fire artillery and mortars into Sarajevo from Bosnian Serb lines. On a few occasions, it was concentrated artillery fire in a specific area, but most of the time it was sporadic and individual shells. As to personal evidence, you could hear this going on if you were in Sarajevo. Secondly is that there was reports from the UNMOs every day reporting the -- the amount of incoming and outgoing artillery fire. So it is a matter of record that that shell-fire was going on. And the deductions that I described a few minutes ago are the basis of consideration of those facts that there were indisputably single sporadic shells being fired continually throughout the five months that I was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you indicate where exactly you objected against the admission of paragraph 90, which is the very basis of -- in your response? Page and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have to get the response. I do not have it in front of me, Your Honours. I apologise, since I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We cannot find it at this moment. Apart from that, in paragraph 90 the witness describes the impression they gained at the time. He has linked it now to certain events and reports that were given to him. Under those circumstances, without having found paragraph 90 in your response as objected to, Mr. Vanderpuye is allowed to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just note, and I'm sure Mr. Ivetic is well aware of this, that the witness has a rather extensive background in matters concerning military artillery --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I said that you could proceed, and we were not at this moment triggering submissions on experience and how that worked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of your experience in Sarajevo, Mr. Tucker, what was the purpose, as best as you could determine, of the type of shelling that you saw, this punitive or random shelling that you saw occurring in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't that -- the purpose of the shelling was in paragraph 90. Is there anything new or do you want the witness, who has testified to the accuracy of his statement, to say it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to know if the witness has anything new to add to his statement, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is in paragraph 23 which we did object to precisely for this military purpose. That's objection A, paragraph 5(a) of our response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read in (a): "Paragraph 23, the second type of fire was single shells landing around the city to no military purpose, and they were not fired in support of attacks or to defend." Do you expect on the Chamber to search for the whole of your response to see whether anything is linked to paragraph 23?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm saying that the question that was just asked goes paragraph 23 which we have objected to which I have just put forth in front of Your Honours. It is my job to search. I have done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vanderpuye, and any reason to -- of course, Mr. Tucker, as far as the purpose of this shelling is concerned, the punitive or random shelling, would you like to add anything to your statement or is what you say in your statement your -- what you wanted to comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no -- nothing further to add, nothing new to add to what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you in your preparation for this testimony, did you give any suggestion to the Prosecution that you would like to add something as far as the purpose of this random or terrorist shelling is concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you may proceed. And I take it that you've carefully listened to both my questions and the answers given by the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have, Mr. President. And I'm not sure if I understand the Court's ruling. Is it that the Prosecution is not allowed to elicit evidence from the witness that is outside the scope or outside the specific words of the 92 ter statement, or is it that -- or is it that the particular question that I'm putting to the witness in terms of its substance is inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It is because we expect you not to be repetitious in your examination of the witness. What is in the statement doesn't need to be asked again to hear the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask it this way then. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, ask something else I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did the shelling that you observed, Mr. Tucker, appear to follow part of a broader plan in respect of the Bosnian Serb leadership's objectives concerning Sarajevo, Srebrenica, Cerska, and Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He's asking for the witness to speculate and to give expert testimony for which this witness has not been qualified before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, this question is too broad. If you want to explore these matters, then please do not ask the witness about whether he has any knowledge of a broader plan and what it was -- what this knowledge is based on and then compare it. But this question as phrased now is too broad. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In respect of the shelling and sniping that you observed in Sarajevo, Mr. Tucker, did what you observe appear to follow any plan on the part of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I cannot comment on what plans the Bosnian Serb leadership may or may not have had. What I can comment is that it was consistent behaviour across many parts of the conflict area and that similar use of artillery was made in many places.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the use of that artillery in relation to what you've commented on in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you want to ask the witness what he perceived to be the purpose of that artillery. What the purpose is depends on the one who -- who fires the artillery. If the witness formed any opinion about what he saw and heard, of course we can ask the witness. Did you -- did you form any opinion as to what may have been the purpose of what you saw happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our perception of what the reason for using artillery in that way was that it was intended to frighten and terrorise the population and to try and make them -- motivate them to leave the area of where that shelling was taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vanderpuye, is this the -- the answer or the information that you sought from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I can tell you that this is also in the statement clearly expressed. So we don't want to hear the same evidence as we found already in his statement, which was admitted. That's the whole purpose of 92 ter. Please keep this in the back of your mind, and you may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You travelled to Eastern Bosnia, as you've indicated. Did you see any evidence of a practice of burning down the houses of the fleeing population by Bosnian Serb -- by the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I saw some evidence in parts of the enclaves where I travelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in respect of those observations, were you able to draw any conclusions as to what the purpose of those actions was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, if he's asking for conclusions, I would say this witness has not been properly tendered under Rule 94 bis to render expert-type conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could ask the witness whether he formed any opinion about what the purpose of those actions was. That's a factual question, whether the witness did form such an opinion. Did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw facts on the ground. In other words, houses whose roofs had been burnt, where the furniture had been destroyed, where the ovens and the fridges had been thrown out into the -- into the garden, and where cattle, sheep, pigs had been locked in the buildings in order to defecate in the buildings. That I saw in a number of areas. Now, what the purpose and reason for doing that was, we surmised that the reason was to frighten people who were living in those houses previously into leaving and not coming -- and make it difficult for them to consider coming back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did it ever come to your mind that it would serve a military purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unless you consider the military purpose to be the clearance of people out of an area that you wanted to control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but no other -- you could not detect any other military purpose when you formed your opinion --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- about what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two types of damages that you could observe to houses. You could see houses that had no roofs, because all the roofs in Bosnia were wood, and which were in the condition I just described to you. Those houses did not have damage, bullet holes, to the side of houses. You then had other houses which were damaged with bullet holes and shell holes in the side of the houses. Those were houses where military fighting and military combat had taken place, and you could always tell immediately, ah, that house has been ethnically cleansed, whereas the other house with the holes in the side, that one is where military combat and fighting had actually taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to show the witness 65 ter 3402.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again this document was given to us notice for this witness at 5.00 in the afternoon yesterday and was not within the seven-day guidance of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what Mr. Ivetic is talking about. There is very clear, very clear guidance on the record of these proceedings. At transcript page 2160, the Court gave very specific guidance which says as follows: "The parties are encouraged to send lists of documents to be used during examination-in-chief as early as possible." In this case Mr. Ivetic received it in excess of 30 days before this witness testified. "The Chamber would expect that a first list of documents be sent not later than seven days prior to the witness's testimony," which Mr. Ivetic received. "Such a list could then be complemented," and I quote, "complemented at a later stage following any proofing of the witness," which is precisely the circumstances under which Mr. Ivetic received the documents in this case. Furthermore, in relation to the witness's testimony, the document I propose to put to the witness relates specifically to his direct and personal observations during his time in Bosnia. Moreover, as Mr. Ivetic is fully aware, this witness has specific training and expertise, I might add, in artillery matters which are the direct subject matter of his testimony and which the Chamber has previously given guidance is an appropriate basis upon which to put questions to the witness concerning his opinions. I don't know what Mr. Ivetic is objecting to, and I don't know on what basis he's making these objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- before I give an opportunity to Mr. Ivetic to respond, would that mean that any document you would have used in proofing where you would normally expect it to be considered for the use with the witness well in advance that -- so there is an unlimited realm of new documents in the complement -- the complementary part of the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. You can see me shaking my head. The number of documents that I sent to Mr. Ivetic are probably not more than six. Number one. Number two, with respect to the document that is the 16th Assembly minutes, 16th Session Assembly minutes concerning General Mladic's speech, I sent them specifically the pages references that I would use. It's an enormous document. I think it's 50 or 60 pages. I gave them the specific page references concerning that. And I do understand the Court's concern about flooding the Defence at the last minute, but this is a far cry from that. In fact, of the documents that Mr. Ivetic has received, they probably don't total, with the exception of -- there is one UN document that is just coming up on the screen, with the exception of that document they probably don't total more than 20 pages all put together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection is very clear. It's based on the guidance and the ruling that Your Honours have given on the prior document. It is correct that six documents were disclosed to us for this witness at 5.00 p.m. yesterday. I'm stating facts. I'm not stating anything that's inaccurate. The witness list for this witness that Your Honours identified as being rather lengthy has approximately 58 documents on it, and in addition to those 58 documents we received 6 documents yesterday at 5.00. I am objecting to it and I will abide by whatever Your Honours' order is on this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, any response to Mr. Vanderpuye's observation about to complement the list with documents which arose during proofing?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Your Honour, that's why I said I don't know what the guidance is. I'm asking Your Honours, if I'm wrong in understanding your guidance, please tell me that I'm wrong and I will then tailor my approach differently to this witness and other witnesses. I'm trying to find out how we're supposed to be acting in this courtroom, what rules we're supposed to be following, and I'm trying to adhere to them, and I would also like to -- I'd be remiss if I didn't point out that since now the Prosecution has indicated they are relying upon the expertise of this witness, I would ask the testimony to be barred because Rule 94 bis has not been adhered to for this witness to provide expert testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're mixing up two different matters, isn't it. Let me just consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to add one thing and just to clarify one thing: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I apologise interrupting you. Mr. Ivetic indicated these documents were disclosed to him yesterday. In fact, these documents were disclosed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, now there's no --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: A long time ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: They were indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, Mr. Vanderpuye, I think there's no issue about when they were disclosed. There's an issue about when notice was given that you would use them with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the issue - that's -- that became clear. Whatever language was used by Mr. Ivetic, I have not checked that. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, the Chamber considers that what comes new in proofing, that is documents of which the Prosecution -- Prosecution -- documents the Prosecution could not link to that witness any earlier than during proofing. Now, therefore, we wonder when we have a statement of the witness, and let's return to the one we have ruled on already, that if the witness statement is clear and if that other document contains, as you suggest, information which is fully consistent with the witness's statement, why is it that you could not link that information any earlier to the witness than one day before his examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the most clear reason is that the documents that I'm using with the witness, first of all, do not directly implicate the witness. They bear upon matters that the witness observed which are directly relevant, and they are directly relevant to those observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the question was why could you not link it, because you're now clearly explained what the link to the witness is, why couldn't you have done that before proofing?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I were to do that, the exhibit list -- or the proposed exhibit list for any given witness could number in the thousands, because if this witness testifies that he -- or, rather, his statement bears upon ethnic cleansing in Eastern Bosnia, that would put a million documents on Mr. Ivetic's exhibit list which could potentially be used with this witness. What we're talking about is something that's far more narrow and far more precise than that, and it has to do with specific observations that he made which did not -- which were not put to him in his prior testimony, which were not put to him at any point prior to the -- prior to the statement that was -- his amalgamated statement, and which were only put to him in proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're able to make a selection of, as you said, six documents, I found a few more but perhaps they had been on the previous list, if you are able to select those for the proofing of the witness, you should have been able to give notice of that a week ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to the Defence, and I take it that you never intended to use a million documents. I take it a bit of an exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But it underscores the point which is that the documents that I disclosed or indicated to Mr. Ivetic that I was going to use are -- they're very limited in number and they're very limited in scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's to avoid precisely the situation where the Defence would be unable, wholly unable, to prepare for the cross-examination of a witness based upon those documents. They are six, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you made that selection to deal with those documents during proofing, and the question of the Chamber is why you didn't make that selection a week ago, because I take it that you have not put all million documents to the witness and then it suddenly emerged that these six were relevant. You have made your own selection and I think the message of the Chamber is that you should have done that before yesterday in the afternoon. I take it that you have a limited number of documents you want to put to the witness during proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have a limited number of documents I want to put to the witness in proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't know what the witness is going to say about those documents until I put them to him in proofing, and so it would be irresponsible for me to put that on an exhibit list to indicated to the Defence to prepare for 500 documents or a million documents or 20 documents or 30 documents without any knowledge whether -- whatsoever whether or not the witness can actually speak to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is exactly the problem that arose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- with respect to the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many documents, not associated exhibits, did you put anew to this witness during proofing?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I believe I've -- actually, no, more than six. I have them on my -- I have indicated that in a proofing note also to Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many. I asked you. You said not six. How many did you put to the witness, new documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you give me a moment, I'll pull up my proofing note and I can take a look and give you an accurate number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In all, Mr. President, I count nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what the issue is, you said that it would be irresponsible to put all those on the list. Now, you would have nine instead of six. The Defence would have had a week to look at those nine documents. It would not be irresponsible. You are talking about huge amounts. In fact, you're telling us that there were nine that you used with the witness during proofing. What you should have done is to give notice of those nine you intended to deal with during proofing to the Defence so that they could prepare for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that the Chamber has misunderstood me. The nine documents I put to the witness were documents that I -- that I vetted before I proofed him. If I were to give the Defence notice of the documents within the potential range of documents I would put to him, it would be utterly ineffective for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you use nine documents during proofing, well, let's say that at the last minute you have to make up your mind finally whether there would have been 15 or, but that is reality. You use a very limited number of documents with the witness during proofing. At that moment you shouldn't wait until the day before the testimony starts, but you should give notice to the Defence already at that early stage, and that would not be irresponsible. I think that would be very responsible. And I would like to leave it to that at this very moment. Let's now then rule on the document. You wanted to put to the witness which one again, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 340 -- I think it's 3402.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3402. Yes. Yes. Any specific link with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that the subject matter, of course. Everything in the former Yugoslavia has to do with the -- let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, there are some matters that are specifically linked to this witness, Mr. President, and those -- if you'd like, I can give you the paragraphs numbers I intend to show him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm consulting with my colleagues, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, we allow the use of documents only if specific facts are mentioned in that document to which the witness can testify, not about practice of shelling or -- but specific facts. A fact is something that happened on a certain day in a certain area and which is described concretely. If that is the case with 3402, you may proceed. If, however, it's just a report describing the situation in -- human rights in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, that is too general a subject to link it to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. What I'd like to show the witness in this document in particular is paragraph 105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's -- could I invite the witness not yet to look at paragraph 105 of this document. We'll have a look at it, and then we'll see, Mr. -- do we have it on our screen already? I don't think -- well -- yes, we have it. You said paragraph 105. We'll read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I think the witness testified about burning down of houses. If you think that he would have any specific knowledge about what happened in the village of Bradina or -- this is about, by the way, by Croat forces. I do not know whether you're interested in that. It seems to be a bit outside the scope of -- but if you have, again, any specific village, if the witness would have any specific knowledge about that, ask the witness about it and put the document to him. However, the witness testified about what he saw as far as burning houses are concerned, and at this moment the Chamber is unable to identify any specific factual matter in paragraph 105 to which it expects - but we have not proofed the witness, we have only read his statement - we did not -- we're not able to identify any specific factual matter where we would expect the witness to have any personal knowledge or observation. Unless you find something like that --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. I do. That's the reason why I've asked the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's the first sentence in the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is not a specific factual matter, but that is a general statement, and therefore if that's what you want to ask questions about, then you are not allowed to use this document which you have given notice of only yesterday to the Defence. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is it a question of relevance, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said this is a ruling. You are not allowed. You have given this document yesterday to the Defence, whereas you should have done that a week ago, and you haven't done that, and that's the reason why --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the Chamber ruled as it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you testified a minute ago about having observed evidence that houses were burnt during your period in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you tell us what information you had, if any, about how widespread that particular kind of conduct was in the areas that you yourself visited or were aware of?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I personally saw the evidence after the action of houses having been burnt in the way previously described in the area between Sarajevo and Kiseljak. I saw it in the area around Srebrenica and a number of villages in the Srebrenica pocket. I saw it later in the area of Mrkonjic Grad in the Banja Luka area. That's what I personally saw myself. I also saw it in the areas around the Lasva Valley. In addition to that, there were media reports and television pictures which were taken during the -- at the time when people were actually being evicted from their houses. I also saw journalist reports from journalists who had been present and seen these actions taking place. All of those together built up into a consistent picture of what had been happening in those areas which were ethnically cleansed. Sorry, one more place that I actually saw the consequence myself is in the area to the south-west of Banja Luka where there were previously Muslim civilians who had been displaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker. Did you receive any information concerning the shelling or artillery fire directed against hospitals in particular?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and in particular around the two hospitals in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have any dealings -- in fact, let me rephrase that. You did have dealings with Vinko Pandurevic as you've indicated in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you aware of whether or not Vinko Pandurevic engaged in the practice of burning Muslim houses in the areas in which the VRS -- in which the VRS entered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As phrased I believe that the question asked for the witness to speculate as to matters that are -- as to a third party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness is asked about whether he has any knowledge about Vinko Pandurevic engaged in certain practice. That is not asking for speculation. That is exploring with the witness whether he has any knowledge of it, and of course then the next question would be on what base he gained that knowledge. Do you have any knowledge about Vinko Pandurevic being engaged in the practice of burning Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know or have any specific knowledge whether Vinko Pandurevic engaged in that. What I do know is that he was the VRS commander in areas where that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to show the witness 65 ter 9059.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the Chamber's benefit, I would direct -- it is one such document, and I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's one such document. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I would direct the Chamber to the last line of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last line. Yes. So what we'd like to know is whether the witness has any specific knowledge about Konjevic Polje and whether or not houses were burned there. Could we first ask whether the witness has any knowledge about that. That can be done even without using the document at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, do you have any knowledge of houses being burnt in the area of Konjevic Polje during the period of time that you were there, obviously, or if you have any information concerning whether or not houses were burned in that area?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I do not have specific knowledge of houses being burnt in Konjevic Polje because I was there before the VRS seized that -- that territory. Afterwards I went through that area, but there had been quite heavy fighting and I could not determine because I didn't spend time looking at the houses to see whether it was burnt or whether it was combat damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This determines the fate of this document, Mr. Vanderpuye, again without prejudice, but for using it with this witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of what you observed concerning the burning of houses, given your extensive military experience, is that something that you would expect to have occurred in the absence of a chain of command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is quintessential expert testimony. It has not been tendered and subjected to Rule 94 bis and I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me re-read the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer to this question, Mr. Vanderpuye, the Chamber considers not to assist it in whatever ways it go, whether he did expect it or whether he did not expect it. It's not a question to which the answer would assist us in making the determinations we have to. Please proceed. So the witness is not -- doesn't have to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
