utterances.text: You were present in the area of Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica around March of 1993, and in respect of your visit there, did you see evidence of a campaign being carried out by the Bosnian Serb military to remove the Muslim population from those areas?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's a matter of a legal conclusion that I believe is the purview of the Chamber to determine this. He can testify to what he saw. I don't think he can draw conclusions of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you can -- whether it's conclusion or not -- a witness can develop a personal opinion on the consistency of what he sees, and that's not a legal conclusion. Now, perhaps the question would have been better phrased slightly different to achieve that purpose. But what Mr. Vanderpuye apparently wanted to ask you is whether you, when observing what happened in the areas covered by the question in March of 1993, whether you saw or whether you formed any opinion about it being a pattern or, rather, loose incidents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, what I saw was reports from the UN military observers who were with General Morillon and myself inside the Srebrenica pocket who were sent out into the area around Srebrenica in order to observe what was happening. Those military observers reported back to me what they saw, and it is those observations that I'm reporting. What those military observers reported seeing was continued sporadic shell-fire of villages on the edge of the perimeter, and over a number of days then a military attack on the ground would follow a number of days of sporadic shell-fire, and then the Serb forces would seize that particular village, and this would then proceed to the next village. This behaviour, and this is observable fact that we saw on the ground, the consequence of these actions by the Bosnian Serb Army was to precondition the civilians living in these villages that as soon as they started being shelled, one shell every 40 minutes, one shell every two hours, then suddenly two shells, as soon as that started happening to their village, they then knew that they were within a few days going to be attacked by ground forces, and so those civilians then packed up whatever they could carry and then fled away from the Bosnian Serb forces, which meant basically towards the centre of the pocket, which meant basically towards Srebrenica. That was reported to us by the UN military observers in the Srebrenica pocket, and it was described to us many times by refugees who we talked with in Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And on the basis of this information, you considered it to be events according to a pattern.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It appeared to us to be far too consistent for it to be coincidence and that this had to be in some way, shape, or form a deliberate plan of action which was being conducted by the Bosnian Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Vanderpuye. We need another break. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 13 minutes to 2.00. Could the witness first leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, in light of what you said just before the break concerning what appeared to you to be a pattern or not to be a coincidence with respect to the -- to what you observed in Eastern Bosnia, in your statement at paragraph 134 you talk about a counter-offensive being carried out by the Bosnian Serb Army. I was wondering how that figures in to your assessment of the pattern that you just described concerning Eastern Bosnia, Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Srebrenica, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: General Morillon had been told by Dr. Karadzic and other members of the Bosnian Serb government and leaders that the Bosniak, that is the Muslim forces in Eastern Bosnia, had conducted a series of attacks against Bosnian Serb forces and civilians in Eastern Bosnia and had killed a number of civilians, and I believe the number, from recollection, was -- 1.260 was mentioned quite a few times. And that, as a result, the Bosnian Serb forces were taking steps against the eastern enclaves and that is -- was a declared intent by the -- by Dr. Karadzic and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership. That intent was confirmed by reports that we were being given by the Bosnian Muslim leadership about the situation and what was happening in the -- the eastern -- eastern enclaves, and that is why General Morillon was asked by Izetbegovic at the beginning of March to go personally himself to the eastern enclaves in order to establish what was actually going on and in order to ameliorate the terrible situation that he was telling us that Muslim civilians were in and experiencing in these enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Based on what you could observe and what you know or testified about the apparent plan that you observed or lack of coincidence concerning Bosnian Serb intentions towards Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica, did you then or do you now find any credit with respect to the so-called counter-offensive as a result of the events on 7 January 1993, as a basis for what you ultimately observed when you were in Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica in 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: At the time, given what we knew at the time, we had heard the Bosnian Serb leadership from the middle of December onwards declaring that they wished peace, cease-fires, et cetera. That is what we had heard at the time. We then heard the reports about attacks on the eastern enclaves by the Bosnian Serbs, and we heard reports from the Bosnian Serbs that people in the enclaves had carried out attacks out of the enclaves. Given what we knew at the time, we could see for a fact that a campaign had been initiated by the Bosnian Serbs in order to seize the eastern enclaves. What I know after the fact from documents from the VRS army which have been shown to me by the Office of the Prosecution are documents from the VRS army which show that the attack on the eastern enclaves in order to seize these eastern enclaves had in fact been planned and ordered in November of 1992 that had been -- that they had ordered a tactical halt to the attacks in the middle of December in order to not represent to the international community that they're being aggressive, and that they were ordered to continue the attacks in January and February. Those are documents which I was shown after the event. I obviously did not have -- General Morillon obviously did not have that information at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker. In relation to your service in Bosnia, I understand that you received a commendation, and I wondered if you might tell the Trial Chamber just a little bit about that.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I was awarded the military cross for halting or preventing the last Serb military attempt to capture Srebrenica around the 18th or 19th of -- of March when General Morillon had left the enclave in order to go to Zvornik in order to get the UNHCR convoy, humanitarian convoy, which had been blocked in Zvornik for many weeks. He left me at the front line, at the Yellow Bridge between Srebrenica and Bratunac, in order to "keep the front line open." And by that he meant the warring factions, all parties, repeatedly used the excuse oh, there is fighting going on, as a reason for not allowing humanitarian aid convoys to pass, and General Morillon wished me to stay there in order to observe what was going on and be a presence on the ground to try and make sure that that excuse would not be used again. What actually happened in the six hours between General Morillon leaving the Yellow Bridge and returning with the UNHCR convoy six hours or so later was that as soon as General Morillon -- as the vehicle left, about 15 minutes later a column of tanks and armoured vehicles came out of woods and tried to cross the Yellow Bridge towards Srebrenica, brackets, now that General Morillon was out of the way. I had my armoured personnel carrier parked on the Yellow Bridge which was half destroyed and been filled with rubble. So a track vehicle could bump its way across. A tank could have squeezed around my armoured vehicle, but it would have been risky, and I stood in the way of the leading Serb tank and stood in front of it waving and gesticulating at the commander and the driver not to pass, and I refused to get out of the way. After a standoff for about 15 minutes, this was during a fire-fight where Muslim soldiers behind me and Serb soldiers in the front lines in front of me were firing at each other. The Serb tanks backed off and went into reverse and back into -- back behind Serb lines. This happened a second time a few hours later. It was clear to me that the commander of the tank, the Serb tank company, who was reservist, who spoke good English, actually, he was a teacher, he was not keen at all on pressing forward the attack, which is why me standing in front of his tank -- I mean, he could have just driven over me, but the Serb colonel in the -- on the ground dugout behind the Serb front lines screamed and shouted and ranted and raved at the -- the Serb tank company commander about going into the attack, and there was a lot of shooting going on back and forth and a lot of arguing and shouting and -- but that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tucker. I don't have any further questions for you, and I apologise for some of the procedural interruptions to your testimony. Mr. President, that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Ivetic, it will be you who will cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you'll now be cross examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Tucker - I'll call you Colonel as I believe that is your preference as I've garnered from prior proceedings - prior to your deployment to Sarajevo in 1992, did you have occasion to receive any instruction or training relative to the specific constitutional or political framework of the SFRY or the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We had some training and briefings which were conducted in -- at Monchengladbach with the headquarters before it deployed, where the entire background to the negotiations and discussions which had started back in -- back in March. Was I given a detailed briefing about the intricacies of it? No, I was not. Was I given some briefing about the matter materials? Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you quantify, was it a few hours, a few days? Is there any way to tell us how extensive this training was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The overall briefing -- briefings were carried out in a number of session, and I would guess -- I would estimate that they were probably about a total of three to four days' worth of briefings conducted over a period of about a week and a half, two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. I'm waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. I should have mentioned since we both speak English we should try to pause between question and answer to allow the translators and transcribers to catch up with us. Did this training that you had that you said took about several sessions over a three to four day period, did it all involve the military structure of the JNA, the Territorial Defence system, the Army of Croatia, the Croat Defence Union, the VRS, or the army of BiH? That is to say, did you receive any specific training or instruction as to their structure, operative rules, and history before deploying to Bosnia-Herzegovina in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: We received some briefings. The knowledge of the intelligence organisation of the headquarters with which I deployed to Bosnia of the specifics in the former Yugoslavia were, of course, limited and were hastily pulled together.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, apart from this training that was imparted to you in that three to four day period, you personally did not have any prior formal education as part of your military or any civil education with respect to the SFRY and the militaries that existed in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: No, not training, just listening to the media as it was obviously one of the top events in the media that was being reported at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe we already have P317 up on the screen. If we could look at the fourth page in English, and it's also the fourth page in the B/C/S, these are paragraphs 15 and 16 of your witness statement that I would like to ask you about. And there we have it on the screen now, sir. In these paragraphs you identify issues that were raised with the Bosnian Serbs, as you say, "after my arrival in the latter part of 1992, we had a number of issues which we were constantly raising with the Bosnian Serbs, and they had a number issues they were constantly raising with us." I want to ask you about that which should be in the same context but which I could not find in your statement. What were the issues that you, in the sense of the UNPROFOR BH command, raising with the Bosnian Muslims during this time period?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: The issues that we were raising with the Bosnian Muslims were that they should also enable freedom of movement of UN forces as they also at times were impeding those or making it difficult; that they should distribute humanitarian aid which was delivered to them by the international community in a free and fair manner; and that they should not provoke incidents by creating attacks which looked as if they had been caused by somebody else. Those were the main ones that we -- we covered with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you, and again I'm talking about the UNPROFOR BH command at that time, raise any issues with the Croatian Army in this context?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: In the mixed military working group around Sarajevo there were three what I would call combatant parties - there were the Bosnian Serbs, there were the Bosnian Muslims, and there were the Bosnian Croats - and it is through that forum that we also had discussions with the Bosnian Croats, and we had similar -- we raised similar issues with them as we did with the Bosnian Muslims, which is to say freedom of movement for humanitarian aid and for the UN. It was the free and fair distribution of humanitarian aid, and it was the prevention of actions, breaking cease-fires, and set up to look as if somebody else had fired upon the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I asked about the Croatian Army and your answer talks about the Bosnian Croats. Would you agree with me that we are talking about two different entities?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There are two different entities, but the -- they were very closely related. The two different entities are the Army of the Republic of Croatia and the Bosnian Croat forces inside Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were repeated accusations that Bosnian Croat army forces were from time to time masquerading as if they were Bosnian Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to take a look at what you just said. I think you've got your words mixed up, but ...

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: You are correct. What I meant is that there were accusations that the -- that forces from the Republic of Croatia came into Bosnia and masqueraded as if they were Bosnian Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And apart from there being just mere accusation, did the UNPROFOR BH command have actual knowledge of the Army of the Republic of Croatia in part having crossed over and being on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, in two -- in two places. One is in the south of Bosnia, in the area of Trebinje north of Dubrovnik; and secondly is in the area that in the UN we called the Orasje pocket which is where forces from the Republic of Croatia crossed the Sava River and came onto the southern side of the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so again I ask my original question: What issues, if any, did the BH command of UNPROFOR raise with the Army of the Republic of Croatia that was known to be on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: My understanding is that those issues were raised with the Croatian republic through UNPROFOR in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could focus on the items listed in paragraph 15 of your statement, you identify among the issues the demilitarisation of Sarajevo. Did that in your parlance include the demilitarisation of the Bosnian Muslim forces in Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: I'm looking for the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It's paragraph 15, and it's the middle of paragraph 15 "... lifting the siege of Sarajevo (demilitarisation and safe corridors)."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: Demilitarisation of Sarajevo was discussed. The other issue which was discussed was the centralisation of heavy weapons away from the front line which at that time was mainly around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, sir, my question for you is when you use that word demilitarisation, did that include in your parlance the demilitarisation of the Bosnian Muslim forces in Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was a proposal which Dr. Karadzic, and I believe General Mladic as well on a couple of occasions, made to General Morillon in November, December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was it something that the UNPROFOR BH command considered to be necessary for demilitarisation; that is to say, demilitarisation of the Bosnian Muslim forces in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was a proposal which General Morillon passed on to the leadership of the Bosnian Muslims in Sarajevo, and General Morillon believed that the complete demilitarisation of the Bosnian Muslims in Sarajevo would not be acceptable to them. General Morillon, nonetheless, passed on the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the end of this paragraph, it would seem that you are also saying the same issues applied to the eastern enclaves and Bihac. And I wanted to ask you was there -- was the UNPROFOR position as you understood it at that time to seek demilitarisation of the Bosnian Muslim forces that were situated within the eastern enclaves and within the municipality of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: It was certainly a proposal from the Bosnian Serb side to demilitarise; in other words, remove all weapons from the Bosnian Muslims in Bihac and in Eastern Bosnia. But again, General Morillon did not believe that such would be acceptable to the Bosnian Muslims and -- but he nonetheless passed on the proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can just ask one more question so we don't lose sight of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did General Morillon believe that the Bosnian Serbs would agree to give up their heavy weapons and demilitarise if the other side in the same region did not demilitarise?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER
utterances.text: There is a difference in demilitarising which to my parlance means handing in all weapons, in other words including small arms, and the centralisation of heavy weapons which leaves small arms in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We can have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes we'll adjourn for the day. Mr. Tucker, before we adjourn, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given already today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow, if that's clear to you. You may follow the usher. Yes. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow Tuesday, the 9th of October, at 9.30 in this same Courtroom I.
